decks.title: Cash Flow Statement — Part 1: Meaning, Cash Equivalents and Classification
goals: Explain the meaning and importance of a cash flow statement under AS 3 (revised)
Identify cash and cash equivalents and recognise what is not a cash flow
Classify cash flows into operating, investing and financing activities
Place the special items in the ISC syllabus: proposed and interim dividends, issue expenses, redemption premium, loans given

slides.heading: Cash Flow Statement
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what the statement shows, what counts as **cash and cash equivalents**, and how every cash flow is classified as **operating**, **investing** or **financing**.

nodes.label: What is not a cash flow

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: profit is not cash, meaning and importance, cash and cash equivalents, what is not a cash flow, the three activities and the special items in the syllabus
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A company can make a profit and still run short of cash. The cash flow statement shows where the cash of a year came from and where it went. In this part we learn its meaning and importance, what counts as cash and cash equivalents, and how every flow is sorted into operating, investing or financing activities.

slides.heading: Profit is not cash

rows: Less: Increase in trade receivables (sales not yet collected)
Less: Increase in inventories (cash tied up in panels and inverters)
Less: Solar panels bought for its own plant
Less: Dividend proposed last year, paid this year

visual.alt: Table showing that an imagined solar company earned a profit before tax of 4,00,000 yet its cash fell by 70,000, because customers had not paid, stock was built up, tax and a dividend were paid and panels were bought
visual.caption: Profit follows the accrual basis; cash moves only when money is received or paid.

slides.narration: Meet Kunzum Solar, an imagined company at Kaza. It earned a profit before tax of rupees four lakh, yet its cash fell by rupees seventy thousand. Customers had not paid, stock had piled up, tax and last year's dividend were paid, and new panels were bought. Profit follows the accrual basis; cash moves only when money actually comes in or goes out.

slides.heading: Meaning of a cash flow statement
bullets: Covers a period: inflows and outflows of **cash and cash equivalents**, grouped into three activities.

rows: cash from the main revenue-earning business, after tax paid
cash spent on and received from long-term assets, investments and loans given
cash raised from and returned to shareholders and lenders
the increase or decrease in cash and cash equivalents
the link with the two balance sheets

visual.alt: Table of the parts of a cash flow statement: operating, investing and financing activities, the net change, and the opening and closing cash and cash equivalents
visual.caption: AS 3 (revised), Cash Flow Statements.

slides.narration: A cash flow statement reports the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period. Accounting Standard three, as revised, groups them into operating, investing and financing activities. Their total is the net change in cash, which links the opening balance in one balance sheet with the closing balance in the next.

slides.heading: Importance of the statement

rows: Explains why cash moved differently from profit
Shows whether operations generate enough cash
Helps plan capital spending, repayments and dividends
Allows comparison less affected by accounting policies

visual.alt: Table of the importance of the cash flow statement: it explains the gap between profit and cash, shows the cash-generating power of operations, helps planning, shows how assets were financed and allows comparison

slides.narration: Why does it matter? It explains why cash moved differently from profit. It shows lenders and suppliers whether the main business generates enough cash to pay its way. It helps directors plan capital spending, repayments and dividends. It shows how new assets were financed. And because cash depends little on accounting policies, it makes comparison easier.

slides.heading: Quick check: profit and cash
slides.narration: Think of the shawl maker’s customers, its stock and its spending on assets. Can cash fall while profit is earned?

slides.heading: Cash and cash equivalents
bullets: **Cash**: cash in hand and demand deposits with banks.
**Cash equivalents**: short-term, highly liquid investments, readily convertible into known amounts of cash, with an insignificant risk of change in value.

rows: Cash in hand; demand deposits with banks
Deposits placed for more than three months
Treasury bills, commercial paper and deposits maturing within three months of acquisition
An old bond close to maturity, bought long ago
Units of overnight or liquid funds with negligible risk

visual.alt: Table of what is and is not included in cash and cash equivalents: cash, demand deposits and investments maturing within three months of acquisition are in; longer deposits, old bonds near maturity and shares are out
visual.caption: Test: short term, highly liquid, a known amount of cash, insignificant risk of change in value.

slides.narration: Cash means cash in hand and money in current accounts. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments that turn into a known amount of cash with little risk. As a rule they mature within three months of the day they were acquired, not three months from the balance sheet date. Shares never qualify, however easily they sell.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: cash and cash equivalents of Baralacha Trekking Gear
slides.body_md: Baralacha Trekking Gear Ltd (imagined, Keylong) lists seven holdings at the year end. Which are cash and cash equivalents?

headers: Holding of Baralacha Trekking Gear Ltd (imagined)
rows: Treasury bills bought on issue, maturing in 90 days
Yes (three months or less from acquisition)
Bank deposit placed for four months
Units of an overnight liquid fund
Listed shares of a hotel company
Debentures bought two years ago, now 40 days from maturity
No (test runs from the date of acquisition)

visual.alt: Worked example table: of seven holdings of an imagined trekking-gear company, cash, the current account, ninety-day treasury bills and an overnight fund qualify, giving cash and cash equivalents of 2,05,000

slides.narration: Baralacha, an imagined company at Keylong, lists seven holdings. Cash in hand and the current account are cash. Ninety-day treasury bills bought on issue and the overnight fund are cash equivalents. The four-month deposit is too long, the shares can change in value, and the old debentures fail because the test runs from the day they were bought. The total is rupees two lakh five thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: the three-month test
slides.narration: Count the maturity from the date the investment was acquired. How many months at most?

slides.heading: What is not a cash flow

rows: Movement within cash and cash equivalents
A 45-day deposit made from the current account
Debentures allotted to the seller of a machine
Bonus shares; a transfer to a reserve
Only as an add-back to profit
Dividend proposed for the current year

visual.alt: Table of items that are not cash flows: switches within cash and cash equivalents, non-cash investing and financing transactions, book transfers, non-cash charges and a dividend proposed for the current year

slides.narration: Some items never appear as flows. Moving money from the current account into a short deposit only changes the make-up of cash and cash equivalents. Debentures allotted to the seller of a machine, or bonus shares, involve no cash and are disclosed in a note. Depreciation appears only as an add-back. And a dividend proposed for the current year has no effect at all.

slides.heading: Three activities, one net change

nodes.label: Net change in cash and cash equivalents
Opening plus net change equals closing

visual.alt: Flow diagram: cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities add up to the net change in cash and cash equivalents, which reconciles opening and closing balances
visual.caption: Three activities, one net change

slides.narration: Every cash flow belongs to one of three activities. Operating activities are the main revenue-earning business. Investing activities are the buying and selling of long-term assets and investments, and loans given. Financing activities change the owners’ capital and the borrowings. Together they make the net change in cash and cash equivalents.

slides.heading: Operating activities

rows: Payments to suppliers of goods and services
Wages, salaries and other employee costs
Income tax paid, unless linked to another activity

visual.alt: Table of operating activities: inflows from customers, royalties and commission; outflows to suppliers and employees and for income tax
visual.caption: The principal revenue-producing activities of the enterprise.

slides.narration: Operating activities are the principal revenue-producing activities of the business. Cash comes in from customers and from royalties, fees or commission. Cash goes out to suppliers and employees. Income tax paid is also operating, because it arises from the profit of the business and cannot easily be split among the activities, unless it is clearly linked to an investing or financing transaction.

slides.heading: Investing activities

rows: Sale proceeds of land, buildings, machinery, patents
Purchase of tangible and intangible fixed assets
Sale of shares or debentures held as investments
Recovery of loans given; interest and dividend received
Loans and advances given to others

visual.alt: Table of investing activities: inflows from sales of fixed assets and investments, loans recovered, interest and dividend received; outflows for assets, investments and loans given
visual.caption: For an enterprise that is not a financial enterprise.

slides.narration: Investing activities concern long-term assets and investments that are not cash equivalents. Buying land, machinery or patents is an outflow; selling them brings cash in. Buying shares or debentures of other companies, or lending to another party, is an outflow, and the recovery of such a loan is an inflow. For an ordinary company, interest and dividend received are investing inflows too.

slides.heading: Financing activities

rows: Issue of equity or preference shares, with premium
Redemption of preference shares or debentures, with any premium
Issue of debentures; long-term and short-term loans raised
Repayment of loans; share issue expenses
Interest paid; dividends paid (last year’s proposed, this year’s interim)

visual.alt: Table of financing activities: inflows from shares, debentures and loans; outflows for redemption with premium, loan repayment, issue expenses, interest and dividends paid

slides.narration: Financing activities change the owners’ capital and the borrowings. Issuing shares with any premium, issuing debentures and raising loans bring cash in. Redeeming preference shares or debentures, together with any premium paid, repaying loans, paying share issue expenses, interest and dividends take cash out. Notice that a premium paid on redemption is cash, even when it is written off against securities premium.

slides.heading: Interest, dividends and tax: it depends on the business

visual.alt: Table of how interest, dividends and tax are classified: for a non-financial enterprise interest and dividend received are investing and paid are financing; for a financial enterprise all except dividend paid are operating; tax is usually operating

slides.narration: For an ordinary trading or manufacturing company, interest and dividend received are investing, and interest and dividend paid are financing. For a bank or an investment company, lending and investing are the main business, so interest received, dividend received and interest paid are operating. Dividend paid is financing for everyone. Income tax paid is usually operating.

slides.heading: Quick check: classify four transactions
slides.body_md: Match each transaction with its place.
slides.narration: For each one ask: is it trading, a long-term asset, a change in capital or borrowing, or no flow at all?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the cash flows of Nathula Tea Traders
slides.body_md: Kupup Tea Traders Ltd (imagined, Rangpo) had nine cash transactions in the year. Classify them and total each activity.

headers: Cash transaction of Kupup Tea Traders Ltd (imagined)
rows: Cash sales and collections from customers
Paid tea gardens and other suppliers
Interest received on a fixed deposit (six months)
Interest paid on those debentures for six months
**Net increase in cash and cash equivalents**

visual.alt: Worked example table: nine cash transactions of an imagined tea trader classified into the three activities, giving operating 1,05,000, investing (2,08,000), financing 2,26,500 and a net increase of 1,23,500

slides.narration: Kupup, an imagined tea trader at Rangpo, had nine cash transactions. Collections, payments to suppliers and staff, and tax are operating, a net inflow of rupees one lakh five thousand. The vehicle and the interest received are investing, an outflow of rupees two lakh eight thousand. The debentures, their interest for six months and the interim dividend are financing, an inflow of rupees two lakh twenty-six thousand five hundred. Cash rose by rupees one lakh twenty-three thousand five hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the special items of Jelepla Cardamom
slides.body_md: Jelepla Cardamom Ltd (imagined, Pedong) asks where seven items of the year belong.

rows: Dividend proposed for last year, approved and paid this year
Dividend proposed by the directors for this year
Premium paid on redemption of debentures
Loan given to a growers’ co-operative
Bonus shares issued out of general reserve

visual.alt: Worked example table: seven special items of an imagined cardamom company; last year's proposed dividend, issue expenses and redemption premium are financing outflows, 1,00,000 in all; the loan and its interest are investing, net (1,41,000); this year's proposed dividend and the bonus issue have no effect

slides.narration: Jelepla, an imagined cardamom company, has seven tricky items. Last year’s proposed dividend, paid this year, the share issue expenses and the redemption premium are financing outflows, rupees one lakh in all. The loan to the growers and its interest are investing. This year’s proposed dividend is only a contingent liability, and the bonus issue involves no cash, so neither appears.

slides.heading: Quick check: count the cash equivalents
slides.narration: Pick out cash, the current account and the short investments; leave out the long deposit and the shares.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents, by activity (AS 3 revised)
Maturity of three months or less from acquisition; insignificant risk; never shares
Switches within cash equivalents; non-cash deals; this year’s proposed dividend
Main business, including income tax paid
Fixed assets, investments, loans given, interest and dividend received
Shares, debentures, loans, issue expenses, redemption premium, interest and dividends paid

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the statement, cash equivalents, what is not a cash flow, and the three activities

slides.narration: To sum up: the cash flow statement explains the change in cash and cash equivalents over a year. Cash equivalents mature within three months of acquisition and carry little risk. Switches within cash, non-cash deals and this year’s proposed dividend are not flows. Every flow is operating, investing or financing, and interest and dividends follow the nature of the business.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Apply the **three-month** test from the date of **acquisition**; shares are never cash equivalents.
For a **non-financial** company: interest and dividend **received** are investing; **paid** are financing.
Last year’s **proposed** dividend paid this year is a financing **outflow**; this year’s proposal has **no effect**.
Share issue expenses and premium on redemption are **financing** outflows.
In a classification answer, name the **activity** and say **inflow** or **outflow**.
slides.narration: In the exam, apply the three-month test from the date of acquisition, and remember that shares never qualify. For an ordinary company, interest and dividend received are investing; paid are financing. Last year’s proposed dividend paid this year is an outflow; this year’s proposal has no effect. Issue expenses and redemption premiums are financing. Always say inflow or outflow.

decks.title: Cash Flow Statement — Part 2: Preparation by the Indirect Method, with Adjustments
goals: Work out net profit before tax, treating the previous year’s proposed dividend, the interim dividend and the current proposal correctly
Adjust profit for depreciation, amortisation, sale of assets, provision for doubtful debts, finance costs and working capital
Use working accounts for fixed assets, accumulated depreciation, investments, provision for tax and securities premium
Prepare the investing and financing sections and check the statement against the change in cash

slides.heading: Preparing the statement: the indirect method
slides.body_md: Part 2 — from two balance sheets and additional information to a complete **cash flow statement**, ending with the **cash check**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: rebuild net profit before tax, adjust non-cash and non-operating items and working capital, deduct tax paid, add investing and financing flows, and check against the change in cash
visual.caption: The indirect method, step by step

slides.narration: Now we prepare the statement. We are given two balance sheets and some additional information. We rebuild net profit before tax, adjust it to reach cash from operating activities, use working accounts to find the investing and financing flows, and finish with a check: the net change must equal the change in cash between the two balance sheets.

slides.heading: The format at a glance

headers: Cash Flow Statement for the year ended …
rows: Add: non-cash charges and finance costs; Less: non-operating income
Add / Less: changes in current assets and current liabilities
**Cash generated from operations**; Less: income tax paid
**B. Net cash from (used in) investing activities**
**C. Net cash from (used in) financing activities**
**Net increase or decrease (A + B + C)**; add opening cash and cash equivalents
**Cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year**

visual.alt: Skeleton of a cash flow statement by the indirect method: operating section from net profit before tax to net cash from operating activities, then investing and financing, the net change and the closing balance

slides.narration: The operating section begins with net profit before tax, adds back and deducts the adjustments to reach operating profit before working capital changes, adjusts for working capital to reach cash generated from operations, and deducts tax paid. Then come investing and financing. The three totals give the net change, which, added to opening cash, must give closing cash.

slides.heading: Our case company: Khardung Thermal Wear Ltd

rows: Balance in the Statement of Profit and Loss

visual.alt: Comparative balance sheet of the imagined Khardung Thermal Wear Ltd: totals 25,55,000 and 21,45,000; cash and cash equivalents rose from 1,98,000 to 3,74,000
visual.caption: An imagined company; current year first, in the Schedule III order.

slides.narration: Meet Khardung Thermal Wear, an imagined company at Panamik. Its balance sheet total grew from rupees twenty-one lakh forty-five thousand to rupees twenty-five lakh fifty-five thousand, and its cash and cash equivalents rose from rupees one lakh ninety-eight thousand to rupees three lakh seventy-four thousand. We also know that it issued shares at a premium, redeemed some debentures at a premium, sold a machine and some investments, and paid two dividends.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: net profit before tax
slides.body_md: Khardung (imagined): surplus up ₹90,000; ₹60,000 transferred to general reserve; dividend proposed for 2024-25 paid ₹1,20,000; interim dividend ₹75,000; tax provided ₹1,10,000; dividend proposed for 2025-26 ₹1,50,000.

rows: Balance in the Statement of Profit and Loss, 31 March 2026
Add: Provision for tax made during the year

visual.alt: Working of net profit before tax of Khardung: increase in surplus 90,000, plus the transfer to reserve, last year's proposed dividend and this year's interim dividend, plus the provision for tax, gives 4,55,000
visual.caption: The dividend of ₹1,50,000 proposed for 2025-26 is not added.

slides.narration: The balance sheet shows only the profit kept back. Start with the increase in surplus, rupees ninety thousand. Add back what was taken out of this year’s profit: the transfer to reserve, last year’s proposed dividend paid this year, and the interim dividend. That gives profit after tax of rupees three lakh forty-five thousand. Add the tax provided, and net profit before tax is rupees four lakh fifty-five thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: rebuild the profit
slides.body_md: Work out net profit before tax.
slides.narration: Start from the rise in surplus and add back every appropriation made during the year, then the tax.

slides.heading: Dividends: the ISC rule

rows: Proposed for the previous year, paid this year
Interim dividend for this year, paid

visual.alt: Table of the treatment of dividends: last year’s proposed dividend and this year’s interim dividend are added back to profit and shown as financing outflows; this year’s proposed dividend has no effect; dividend received is deducted in operating and shown under investing
visual.caption: As the ISC syllabus states: previous year’s proposed dividend is an outflow; the current year’s has no effect.

slides.narration: Dividends need care. The dividend proposed for last year is approved and paid this year, so it is added back in the profit working and shown as a financing outflow. The interim dividend is treated the same way. The dividend proposed for this year is only a contingent liability: Khardung’s proposal of rupees one lakh fifty thousand is neither added back nor shown.

slides.heading: Quick check: last year’s proposal
slides.narration: Was last year’s dividend paid out of this year’s surplus, and did cash leave this year?

slides.heading: Adjusting for non-cash and non-operating items

headers: Add back (reduced profit, no operating cash out)
Deduct (raised profit, not operating cash in)
rows: Depreciation; patents, goodwill or other intangibles written off
Profit on sale of fixed assets or investments
Loss on sale of fixed assets or investments
Increase in provision for doubtful debts
Interest on debentures and loans (finance costs)
Decrease in provision for doubtful debts

visual.alt: Table of adjustments to net profit before tax: add back depreciation, amortisation, losses on sale, an increase in provision for doubtful debts and finance costs; deduct profits on sale, interest and dividend received and a decrease in the provision

slides.narration: Next, undo the items in profit that are not operating cash. Add back depreciation, patents or goodwill written off, losses on selling assets, an increase in the provision for doubtful debts, and interest on debentures and loans. Deduct profits on sale and interest or dividend received, which belong to investing. The result is operating profit before working capital changes.

slides.heading: Provision for doubtful debts

rows: Increase in provision for doubtful debts (non-cash charge)

visual.alt: Table comparing two ways of treating the provision for doubtful debts at Khardung: adding back the increase of 3,000 and deducting the rise in gross receivables gives the same cash effect as deducting the rise in net receivables
visual.caption: Either method gives the same cash figure; show one.

slides.narration: When receivables are shown gross with the provision deducted, add back an increase in the provision as a non-cash charge and deduct the rise in gross receivables. At Khardung the provision rose by rupees three thousand. Working with net receivables instead gives exactly the same cash effect, so either method earns full marks. Use one, not both.

slides.heading: Quick check: the provision
slides.narration: Did any cash leave the business when the provision was increased?

slides.heading: Working-capital changes
bullets: Compare each current item in the two balance sheets.
Provision for tax and borrowings are **not** working-capital items here.

visual.alt: Table of the working-capital rule: an increase in a current asset is deducted and a decrease added; an increase in a current liability is added and a decrease deducted
visual.caption: Cash and cash equivalents, provision for tax and borrowings are dealt with elsewhere.

slides.narration: Then adjust for current assets and current liabilities. If inventories or receivables rise, cash is tied up, so deduct the rise; if they fall, add. Current liabilities work the other way: a rise in trade payables means bills not yet paid, so add it; a fall means they were paid off, so deduct it.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: operating activities of Khardung
slides.body_md: Net profit before tax, the adjustments, the working-capital changes and tax paid, from the balance sheets and the working accounts.

rows: Add: Loss on sale of machinery
Add: Increase in provision for doubtful debts
Less: Profit on sale of non-current investments

visual.alt: Operating section of Khardung: net profit before tax 4,55,000, operating profit before working capital changes 6,17,500, cash generated 5,63,500, tax paid 90,000, net cash from operating activities 4,73,500

slides.narration: For Khardung, net profit before tax of rupees four lakh fifty-five thousand, with depreciation, the loss on the machine, the patents written off, the provision and the debenture interest added back, and the investment profit and dividend taken out, gives rupees six lakh seventeen thousand five hundred. After working capital, cash generated is rupees five lakh sixty-three thousand five hundred. Less tax paid of rupees ninety thousand, operating activities bring in rupees four lakh seventy-three thousand five hundred.

slides.heading: Working account: machinery at cost

rows: Accumulated Depreciation A/c (on the machinery sold)
Statement of Profit and Loss (loss on sale)

visual.alt: Machinery account of Khardung at cost: the machine sold leaves at cost against its accumulated depreciation, sale price and loss; purchases are the balancing figure, 4,20,000
visual.caption: Working account at cost.

slides.narration: The machinery account is kept at cost. The machine sold, costing rupees one lakh twenty thousand, leaves against its accumulated depreciation of rupees seventy thousand, the sale price of rupees forty-two thousand and a loss of rupees eight thousand. The amount needed to reach the closing balance, rupees four lakh twenty thousand, is the machinery bought during the year.

slides.heading: Working account: accumulated depreciation

rows: Statement of Profit and Loss (depreciation for the year, balancing figure)

visual.alt: Accumulated depreciation account of Khardung: opening 3,50,000, transfer on sale 70,000, closing 4,10,000; depreciation for the year is the balancing figure, 1,30,000

slides.narration: Accumulated depreciation starts at rupees three lakh fifty thousand. The depreciation on the machine sold, rupees seventy thousand, is transferred out. To reach the closing balance of rupees four lakh ten thousand, this year’s depreciation must be rupees one lakh thirty thousand. That figure is added back in the operating section.

slides.heading: Working account: provision for tax

rows: Statement of Profit and Loss (provision for the year)

visual.alt: Provision for tax account of Khardung: opening 70,000 plus provision 1,10,000 less closing 90,000 gives tax paid of 90,000

slides.narration: The provision for tax starts at rupees seventy thousand, and rupees one lakh ten thousand is provided this year. The closing balance is rupees ninety thousand, so the tax actually paid is rupees ninety thousand. The provision was added through net profit before tax; the tax paid is deducted at the end of the operating section.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: investing activities of Khardung
slides.body_md: Machinery bought (working account); machinery sold for ₹42,000; investments costing ₹1,00,000 sold for ₹1,12,000; investments bought (balancing figure); dividend received ₹18,000.

rows: Proceeds from sale of non-current investments

visual.alt: Investing section of Khardung: machinery bought 4,20,000, machinery sold 42,000, investments bought and sold, dividend received; net cash used 2,88,000

slides.narration: Khardung bought machinery for rupees four lakh twenty thousand and new investments for rupees forty thousand. It received rupees forty-two thousand for the old machine, rupees one lakh twelve thousand for investments and a dividend on its holdings. Net cash used in investing is rupees two lakh eighty-eight thousand. The full sale prices appear here; the loss and profit were adjusted in operating.

slides.heading: Working account: securities premium

rows: Bank A/c (share issue expenses written off)
Bank A/c (premium on shares issued, balancing figure)

visual.alt: Securities premium account of Khardung: opening 50,000, issue expenses 8,000 and redemption premium 5,000 written off, closing 67,000; premium received on the new shares is the balancing figure, 30,000

slides.narration: Securities premium hides a figure. Khardung wrote off share issue expenses and the premium on redeeming debentures against it. Debiting both, the premium received on the new shares is the balancing figure, rupees thirty thousand. So the share issue brought in rupees three lakh thirty thousand, even though the premium balance rose by only rupees seventeen thousand.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: financing activities of Khardung
slides.body_md: Shares issued at a premium; issue expenses paid; debentures redeemed at a premium of five per cent on the first of October; interest paid half-yearly; two dividends paid.

rows: Proceeds from issue of equity shares (including securities premium)

visual.alt: Financing section of Khardung: shares issued with premium 3,30,000, issue expenses, debentures redeemed at a premium, interest and two dividends paid; net cash used 9,500

slides.narration: Khardung raised rupees three lakh thirty thousand from shares and paid issue expenses. It redeemed debentures at a premium, paying rupees one lakh five thousand, and paid interest of rupees thirty-one thousand five hundred, worked half-year by half-year on the debentures outstanding. With last year’s proposed dividend and the interim dividend, net cash used in financing is rupees nine thousand five hundred.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the treatment
slides.body_md: Match each item with its treatment.
slides.narration: For each item, ask what it did to profit and which activity its cash belongs to.

slides.heading: The complete statement and the cash check

rows: Add: Loss on sale of machinery
Add: Increase in provision for doubtful debts
Less: Profit on sale of non-current investments
Proceeds from sale of non-current investments
Proceeds from issue of equity shares (including securities premium)
**Net increase in cash and cash equivalents (A + B + C)**
Add: Cash and cash equivalents at the beginning of the year
**Cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year**

visual.alt: Complete cash flow statement of Khardung: operating 4,73,500, investing (2,88,000), financing (9,500), net increase 1,76,000, opening 1,98,000, closing 3,74,000
visual.caption: The net increase equals closing minus opening cash and cash equivalents: the cash check.

slides.narration: Put the three sections together. Operating activities brought in rupees four lakh seventy-three thousand five hundred; investing used rupees two lakh eighty-eight thousand; financing used rupees nine thousand five hundred. The net increase is rupees one lakh seventy-six thousand. Added to the opening cash of rupees one lakh ninety-eight thousand, it gives rupees three lakh seventy-four thousand, exactly the closing balance. If your statement does not agree, a figure is missing or misplaced.

sections.heading: 3. Classification into three activities
sections.body_md:
**Operating activities** — the principal revenue-producing activities and other activities that are not investing or financing: receipts from customers, royalties, fees and commission; payments to suppliers and employees; income tax paid (unless specifically identified with investing or financing).

**Investing activities** — acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and of investments not included in cash equivalents: purchase and sale of land, buildings, machinery, patents; purchase and sale of shares and debentures of other enterprises; loans and advances made to others and their recovery; interest and dividend received (non-financial enterprise).

**Financing activities** — activities that change the size and composition of owners’ capital and borrowings: issue of equity and preference shares (with premium); issue of debentures and raising of loans; redemption of preference shares and debentures (with any premium); repayment of loans; share issue expenses; interest and dividends paid.

**Interest and dividends:** for a **non-financial** enterprise, interest and dividend received are investing and interest and dividend paid are financing; for a **financial** enterprise, interest paid, interest received and dividend received are operating, and dividend paid is financing.

sections.heading: 4. The format and net profit before tax
sections.body_md:
The statement is prepared by the **indirect method**: the operating section starts from net profit before tax and adjusts it; investing and financing sections list gross receipts and payments.

**Step 1 — net profit before tax** (working note). The balance sheet shows only the retained part of profit, so rebuild it:

Net profit before tax = (closing − opening balance in the Statement of Profit and Loss) + transfers to reserves (general reserve, capital redemption reserve) + dividends paid during the year (previous year’s proposed dividend and this year’s interim dividend) + provision for tax made during the year.

The dividend **proposed for the current year** is not added: it is a contingent liability, not an appropriation of this year’s surplus.

*Not in the ISC 2027 syllabus:* extraordinary items and refund of tax, transactions relating to capital reserve, the adjusted Profit and Loss Account method and the direct method of operating cash flow.

sections.heading: 5. Operating activities: adjustments and working capital
sections.body_md:
**Step 2 — non-cash and non-operating items.**
- **Add:** depreciation; amortisation (goodwill, patents, trademarks written off); loss on sale of fixed assets or investments; increase in provision for doubtful debts (when receivables are taken gross); interest on debentures and loans (finance costs).
- **Deduct:** profit on sale of fixed assets or investments; interest and dividend received (non-financial enterprise); decrease in provision for doubtful debts.
- Result: **operating profit before working capital changes**.

**Step 3 — working capital.** For each current asset (inventories, trade receivables, prepaid expenses): **increase → deduct, decrease → add**. For each current liability (trade payables, outstanding expenses): **increase → add, decrease → deduct**. Result: **cash generated from operations**. Cash and cash equivalents, provision for tax and borrowings are not part of this step.

**Step 4 — tax.** Deduct **income tax paid** (from the provision for tax account): **net cash from operating activities**.

sections.heading: 6. Investing activities and working accounts
sections.body_md:
**Working accounts** reveal the figures the balance sheets hide:
- **Asset at cost** (with an accumulated depreciation account): the asset sold leaves at cost against its accumulated depreciation, the sale price and the profit or loss; **purchases** are the balancing figure.
- **Accumulated depreciation:** opening + depreciation for the year − depreciation on the asset sold = closing; the **depreciation for the year** is usually the balancing figure.
- **Asset at written-down value:** opening + purchases + profit on sale = sale price + loss on sale + depreciation + closing.
- **Investments:** opening + purchases + profit on sale = sale price + loss on sale + closing.

**Investing section:** purchases (outflows) and full **sale prices** (inflows) of fixed assets, intangibles and investments; loans given (outflow) and recovered (inflow); interest and dividend received. The profit or loss on sale is adjusted only in the operating section.

sections.heading: 7. Financing activities
sections.body_md:
- **Equity shares:** increase in share capital − shares issued to vendors − bonus shares, plus the **premium received** (from the securities premium account, which may also be debited with issue expenses and redemption premiums).
- **Share issue expenses** paid: financing **outflow**, whatever they are written off against.
- **Preference shares and debentures redeemed:** outflow of the face value **plus any premium** paid. A capital redemption reserve created out of profit is a transfer, not a cash flow; add it back in the profit working.
- **Debentures issued and loans raised:** inflows; **repayments:** outflows. Short-term borrowings are financing too.
- **Interest paid** on debentures and loans: work it for the period each balance was outstanding; it is added back in operating and paid under financing.
- **Dividends paid:** previous year’s proposed dividend and this year’s interim dividend (and preference dividend paid) are outflows; this year’s proposed dividend has **no effect**.

**Non-cash** issues (shares or debentures to vendors, bonus shares, conversion) are kept out.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Starting from net profit **after** tax, or forgetting to add back the **transfer to reserve** and the **dividends paid** when rebuilding profit.
- Adding back or showing the dividend **proposed for the current year** (no effect).
- Deducting the **provision** for tax instead of the **tax paid**.
- Showing the **book value** instead of the **sale price** under investing, or forgetting the profit or loss on sale in operating.
- Taking the share proceeds as the rise in share capital and premium, without adding back the **issue expenses** and **redemption premium** written off against the premium.
- Showing a debenture redemption at face value only, leaving out the **premium** paid.
- Treating interest or dividend **received** as operating, or interest **paid** as operating, for a non-financial company.
- Reversing the working-capital rule (an increase in receivables is **deducted**), or adjusting the provision for doubtful debts twice.
- Including **non-cash** transactions or a switch into **cash equivalents** as a flow.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one classification or treatment (MCQ, assertion-reason).
- 2 marks: cash and cash equivalents; net profit before tax; one working account; four classifications.
- 3 marks: one section with its working; a working account with its treatment; six classifications.
- 5 marks (in parts): a section with two working accounts, or a small complete statement (working notes 2, statement 3).
- 8 marks (board question on this unit): a complete statement — net profit before tax 1, working accounts 2, operating 2, investing 1, financing 1, net change and check 1.

**Figures in SOYL practice** are imagined; your paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: The finance director of Lipulekh Herbs Ltd, an imagined company at Dharchula, tells the board that the cash flow statement answers a question which the Statement of Profit and Loss cannot. Which question?

options.text_md: How much profit did the company earn after tax?
Where did the cash and cash equivalents of the year come from, and on what were they spent?
What were the assets and liabilities on the last day of the year?
How was the profit for the year divided between reserves and dividend?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Where did the cash and cash equivalents of the year come from, and on what were they spent? Profit is measured on the accrual basis. The cash flow statement reports the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents, grouped into operating, investing and financing activities; the other options describe the profit statement, the balance sheet and the appropriation of profit.

questions.stem_md: Malshej Agro Ltd, an imagined farm-tourism company at Junnar, holds four investments on 31 March 2026. Which one is a cash equivalent under AS 3 (revised)?

options.text_md: Debentures of another company, bought two years ago, that mature on 31 May 2026
A bank deposit placed for six months on 1 January 2026
Listed equity shares that can be sold on any trading day
Treasury bills bought on 1 March 2026 that mature on 30 April 2026

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Treasury bills bought on 1 March 2026 that mature on 30 April 2026. The three-month test is counted from the date of acquisition, not from the balance sheet date: the treasury bills had about two months to run when bought. The debentures had two years to run when bought, the deposit six months, and shares carry a risk of change in value.

questions.stem_md: Tamhini Rice Mills Ltd, an imagined mill at Mulshi, made four payments of ₹2,00,000 each from its current account in March 2026. Which payment will NOT appear as a cash flow in its cash flow statement?

options.text_md: Placing the money in a 45-day deposit with its bank
Paying farmers for paddy bought on credit
Paying for a new rice-polishing machine
Redeeming debentures at par

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Placing the money in a 45-day deposit with its bank. A 45-day deposit is itself a cash equivalent, so the money only moves from one component of cash and cash equivalents to another and the total does not change. The other three are operating, investing and financing outflows.

questions.stem_md: Khambatki Strawberry Ltd, an imagined company at Wai, bought a cold store for ₹5,00,000 and paid the seller by allotting him its 10% debentures of the same amount. In its cash flow statement this purchase is

options.text_md: an investing outflow and a financing inflow of ₹5,00,000 each
an investing outflow of ₹5,00,000 only
left out, being a non-cash investing and financing transaction
a financing inflow of ₹5,00,000 only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** left out, being a non-cash investing and financing transaction. No cash or cash equivalent changed hands. AS 3 excludes such transactions from the statement and requires them to be disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements.

questions.stem_md: Naneghat Basalt Ltd, an imagined quarrying company at Ghatghar, pays half-yearly interest on its 10% debentures. For this company, which is not a financial enterprise, the interest paid is

options.text_md: an operating outflow
an investing outflow
a financing outflow
not a cash flow, being a charge against profit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a financing outflow. For a non-financial enterprise interest paid is a cost of obtaining finance, so it is shown under financing activities; in the indirect method it is first added back to net profit before tax.

questions.stem_md: Shiradi Investments Ltd, an imagined company at Sakleshpur whose main business is investing in shares and lending money, received dividends on the shares it holds. In its cash flow statement the dividend received is

options.text_md: an operating inflow
an investing inflow
a financing inflow
deducted in the operating section and shown under investing

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** an operating inflow. For a financial enterprise, investing and lending are its principal revenue-producing activities, so interest and dividends received are operating; for a manufacturer they would be investing.

questions.stem_md: Sampaje Spice Ltd, an imagined pepper processor at Sullia, lent ₹1,50,000 for three years to a growers’ co-operative that supplies it. Sampaje is not a financial enterprise. In its cash flow statement the loan is

options.text_md: an operating outflow, because the co-operative is a supplier
a financing outflow
not shown, because the money will be repaid
an investing outflow

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** an investing outflow. Loans and advances made to other parties by an enterprise that is not a financial enterprise are investing activities; their recovery later is an investing inflow, and interest earned on them is an investing inflow too.

questions.stem_md: Aryankavu Cashew Ltd, an imagined processor at Thenmala, paid its advance income tax in four instalments. Unless the tax can be specifically identified with investing or financing activities, it is shown as

options.text_md: a financing outflow
an operating outflow
an investing outflow
an appropriation of profit, left out of the statement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an operating outflow. Tax on income arises from the operations that earn the profit and is usually impracticable to split among the activities, so AS 3 places it under operating activities unless it is clearly linked to another activity.

questions.stem_md:
Kambam Grapes Ltd, an imagined winery near Uthamapalayam, parks its surplus money in listed equity shares.

**Assertion (A):** Kambam’s listed shares are not part of its cash and cash equivalents, however quickly they can be sold.

**Reason (R):** An investment is a cash equivalent only if the amount of cash it will fetch is known and subject to an insignificant risk of change in value.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true and R is the reason for A: share prices move, so the cash the shares will fetch is not known in advance.

questions.stem_md:
Thenmala Rural Bank Ltd is an imagined bank that takes deposits and lends to cashew growers.

**Assertion (A):** The dividend paid by Thenmala Rural Bank to its shareholders is shown under financing activities.

**Reason (R):** For a bank, interest paid on customers’ deposits is shown under operating activities.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. Dividend paid is a return to the providers of capital for every kind of enterprise; R is about interest, which for a bank arises from its main business of borrowing and lending.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Marsimik Pashmina Ltd, an imagined shawl maker, can report a healthy profit for 2025-26 and still close the year with less cash and cash equivalents than it began with.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Profit follows the accrual basis. Cash can still fall when customers have not paid, stock has been built up, assets have been bought or loans and dividends have been paid; explaining that gap is the job of the cash flow statement.

questions.stem_md: Hatkhamba Foods Ltd, an imagined company, treats a short-term investment as a cash equivalent only when it matures within ___ months of the date on which Hatkhamba acquired it.
questions.solution_md: AS 3 (revised) normally treats an investment as having a short maturity when it is three months or less from the date of acquisition.

questions.stem_md: The ISC Accounts syllabus follows the revised Accounting Standard ___, which tells an imagined exporter such as Thal Ghat Pumps Ltd how to classify its cash flows into three activities.
questions.solution_md: Accounting Standard 3 (revised), Cash Flow Statements, issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, governs the statement and its classification.

questions.stem_md:
Rupin Rafting Ltd, an imagined adventure-sports company at Naitwar, lists what it holds on 31 March 2026. How much is its cash and cash equivalents (in ₹)?

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| Cash in hand | 8,000 |
| Balance in current account with a bank | 92,000 |
| Commercial paper bought with 75 days to maturity | 50,000 |
| Bank deposit placed for six months | 1,00,000 |
| Equity shares of a listed company | 40,000 |
| Bank deposit placed for 30 days | 30,000 |
questions.solution_md: Count cash, the current account, the 75-day commercial paper and the 30-day deposit: 8,000 + 92,000 + 50,000 + 30,000 = 1,80,000, that is ₹1,80,000. The six-month deposit is too long and the shares carry price risk.

questions.stem_md:
Thenmala Eco Resorts Ltd, an imagined company, holds the following on 31 March 2026. Which items are its cash and cash equivalents? Give a reason for each and find the total.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| Cash in hand | 15,000 |
| Balance in current account with a bank | 1,35,000 |
| Treasury bills bought on issue, maturing in 60 days | 60,000 |
| Bank deposit placed for one year | 1,50,000 |
| Shares of a listed tea company | 45,000 |
questions.solution_md: Apply the tests to each holding: short maturity from the date of acquisition, readily convertible into a known amount, insignificant risk of change in value.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Item | ₹ | Treatment |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Cash in hand | 15,000 | **Included** (cash) |
| Balance in current account with a bank | 1,35,000 | **Included** (demand deposit) |
| Treasury bills bought on issue, maturing in 60 days | 60,000 | **Included** (maturity within three months of acquisition) |
| Bank deposit placed for one year | 1,50,000 | **Not included** (maturity longer than three months) |
| Shares of a listed tea company | 45,000 | **Not included** (risk of change in value) |

**Cash and cash equivalents** = 15,000 + 1,35,000 + 60,000 = **₹2,10,000**.

marking_scheme.step: Each item placed with a reason

questions.stem_md:
The cashier of Bhor Ghat Rail Parts Ltd, an imagined engineering company at Khopoli, has listed what the company holds on 31 March 2026. Identify, with a reason for each, the items that form part of cash and cash equivalents, and find their total.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| Petty cash | 6,000 |
| Balance in current account | 1,24,000 |
| Bank deposit placed for 60 days | 80,000 |
| Units of an overnight liquid fund | 40,000 |
| Bank deposit placed for nine months | 2,00,000 |
| Debentures of a power company bought last year, maturing in 50 days | 70,000 |
| Trade receivables due within 30 days | 95,000 |
questions.solution_md: The debentures are the trap: the three-month test runs from the day they were bought, not from the balance sheet date.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Item | ₹ | Treatment |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Petty cash | 6,000 | **Included** (cash) |
| Balance in current account | 1,24,000 | **Included** (demand deposit with a bank) |
| Bank deposit placed for 60 days | 80,000 | **Included** (short maturity, fixed amount) |
| Units of an overnight liquid fund | 40,000 | **Included** (highly liquid, insignificant risk of change in value) |
| Bank deposit placed for nine months | 2,00,000 | **Not included** (maturity longer than three months when placed) |
| Debentures of a power company bought last year, maturing in 50 days | 70,000 | **Not included** (maturity counted from the date of acquisition was more than three months) |
| Trade receivables due within 30 days | 95,000 | **Not included** (an operating asset, not an investment) |

**Cash and cash equivalents** = 6,000 + 1,24,000 + 80,000 + 40,000 = **₹2,50,000**.

questions.stem_md: A bank is considering a working-capital loan to Bodimettu Cardamom Ltd, an imagined spice company. State two ways in which Bodimettu’s cash flow statement will help the bank’s credit officer.
questions.solution_md: Link each use to a section of the statement and to the lender’s worry: will the loan be serviced, and how is cash being spent?

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Repaying power from operations:** the net cash from operating activities shows whether Bodimettu’s own trading produces enough cash to pay interest and instalments, without borrowing again or selling assets.
2. **Where the money went:** the investing and financing sections show whether past cash was sunk in long-term assets, used to repay other lenders or paid out as dividends, which tells the officer how the new loan is likely to be used and how tight liquidity will be.

*(Also accepted: it explains why profit and cash differ; it helps forecast future cash needs; it allows comparison with other borrowers, since cash figures depend little on accounting policies.)*

questions.stem_md: The directors of an imagined family company, Changla Dairy Ltd, Durbuk, say: "Our Statement of Profit and Loss shows a profit every year, so a cash flow statement is unnecessary." Give three reasons why the statement is still important for them.
questions.solution_md: Answer the directors directly: three distinct reasons, each showing what the profit statement alone cannot tell them.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Profit is not cash.** Profit is on the accrual basis; credit sales, unpaid expenses, stock build-up, asset purchases and loan repayments make cash differ from profit. The statement explains that gap, item by item.
2. **Liquidity and solvency.** Net cash from operating activities shows whether the dairy can pay suppliers, staff, tax, interest and dividends from its own trading, or is living on borrowings and asset sales.
3. **Planning and decisions.** Past inflows and outflows by activity help the directors forecast cash needs, time capital spending, plan repayments and set a dividend policy the company can afford.

*(Also accepted: easier comparison between years and firms because cash figures depend little on accounting policies; it is required by AS 3 (revised) for companies.)*

questions.stem_md:
The trainee accountant of Fotula Apricot Ltd, an imagined company at Lamayuru, has shown two transactions of 2025-26 in the cash flow statement. Explain why neither belongs there.

(i) Bonus shares of ₹1,50,000 were issued out of the general reserve.
(ii) ₹80,000 was moved from the current account into 60-day treasury bills.
questions.solution_md: For each, ask whether cash left or entered the business, and whether the total of cash and cash equivalents changed.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(i) Bonus issue:** an amount is only transferred from the general reserve to share capital; nothing is received or paid, so it is a **non-cash** transaction and stays out of the statement.

**(ii) Treasury bills:** 60-day treasury bills are themselves a **cash equivalent**. The money has moved from one component of cash and cash equivalents to another; the total is unchanged, so this is **not a cash flow**.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Bonus issue is a non-cash book transfer
(ii) Movement within cash and cash equivalents

questions.stem_md:
Taglang Wool Ltd, an imagined spinning mill at Rumtse, had these three transactions in 2025-26. Its draft cash flow statement shows each of them. State, with reasons, how each should be treated.

(i) Equity shares of ₹4,00,000 were allotted to the seller of a warehouse as its price.
(ii) 9% debentures of ₹2,00,000 were converted into equity shares.
(iii) A 75-day deposit of ₹1,00,000 matured and the money was credited to the current account.
questions.solution_md: Two of the three are non-cash investing or financing transactions; the third is a switch inside cash and cash equivalents.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(i) Shares for a warehouse:** an investing transaction (acquiring an asset) and a financing transaction (issuing shares) with no cash at all. It is a **non-cash transaction**: excluded from the statement and disclosed in a note.

**(ii) Conversion of debentures:** one form of finance is replaced by another; no cash moves. Also a **non-cash** financing transaction, excluded and disclosed.

**(iii) Deposit maturing:** a 75-day deposit is a **cash equivalent**, so its maturity is a movement within cash and cash equivalents; the total does not change and it is **not a cash flow**.

questions.stem_md:
Classify the following cash transactions of Gaimukh Ghat Bottling Ltd, an imagined mineral-water company that is not a financial enterprise, as operating, investing or financing activities, and say whether each is an inflow or an outflow.

(1) Received from customers for bottled water.
(2) Bought a bottling line.
(3) Paid interest on a term loan.
(4) Received interest on a loan given to a dealer.
questions.solution_md: Trading receipts are operating; long-term assets and loans given are investing; interest paid is a cost of finance for a non-financial company.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Transaction | Activity | Inflow or outflow |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Received from customers for bottled water | **Operating** | inflow |
| Bought a bottling line | **Investing** | outflow |
| Paid interest on a term loan | **Financing** | outflow |
| Received interest on a loan given to a dealer | **Investing** | inflow |

questions.stem_md:
Sach Pass Rugs Ltd, an imagined carpet maker at Killar, had the following cash transactions in 2025-26. Classify each as an operating, investing or financing activity.

(1) Purchase of a patent for a new dye.
(2) Wages paid to weavers.
(3) Redemption of preference shares at a premium.
(4) Commission received for selling another mill’s rugs.
(5) Proposed dividend of the previous year paid.
(6) Sale of shares held as a long-term investment.
questions.solution_md: Ask whether each item is trading, a long-term asset or investment, or a change in owners’ capital and borrowings; commission is a trading receipt.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Transaction | Activity |
| --- | --- |
| Purchase of a patent for a new dye | **Investing** |
| Wages paid to weavers | **Operating** |
| Redemption of preference shares at a premium | **Financing** |
| Commission received for selling another mill’s rugs | **Operating** |
| Proposed dividend of the previous year paid | **Financing** |
| Sale of shares held as a long-term investment | **Investing** |

questions.stem_md: Match each cash transaction of an imagined spinning mill, Rumtse Yarns Ltd, in column A with its place in the cash flow statement in column B.

options.text_md: Payment to wool suppliers
Purchase of a carding machine
Redemption of debentures
Purchase of 60-day treasury bills with cash

match_right.text_md: Not a cash flow (switch within cash equivalents)

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Trading is operating, long-term assets are investing, capital and borrowings are financing; a switch between cash and cash equivalents is not a flow.

questions.stem_md:
A new accounts assistant at Kasara Ghat Engineering Ltd, an imagined pump maker at Igatpuri, has to brief the directors.

(a) Explain the meaning of a cash flow statement and of cash equivalents, with one example of a cash equivalent. (2 marks)

(b) Explain the three activities into which AS 3 (revised) classifies cash flows, giving one inflow and one outflow of Kasara Ghat for each. (3 marks)
questions.solution_md: Part (a) needs both definitions and an example; part (b) needs, for each activity, its meaning plus a pump maker’s own inflow and outflow.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A **cash flow statement** shows the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents of an enterprise during a period, classified into operating, investing and financing activities, and reconciles the opening and closing balances. **Cash equivalents** are short-term, highly liquid investments, readily convertible into known amounts of cash and subject to an insignificant risk of change in value, normally maturing within three months of acquisition; for example, a 90-day treasury bill bought on issue.

**(b)**
- **Operating activities:** the principal revenue-producing activities of the company and others that are not investing or financing. Inflow: cash received from customers for pumps. Outflow: payment to suppliers of castings, wages, income tax.
- **Investing activities:** acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and of investments that are not cash equivalents. Inflow: sale proceeds of an old lathe; interest received on investments. Outflow: purchase of a testing rig or of shares of another company; a loan given.
- **Financing activities:** activities that change the size and composition of owners’ capital and borrowings. Inflow: issue of shares or debentures; a term loan raised. Outflow: redemption of debentures; interest and dividends paid.

questions.stem_md: The balance in the Statement of Profit and Loss of Bodimettu Spices Ltd, an imagined company, rose from ₹1,80,000 to ₹2,60,000 in 2025-26. During the year it transferred ₹50,000 to general reserve, paid the dividend of ₹70,000 proposed for 2024-25 and an interim dividend of ₹30,000, and made a provision for tax of ₹90,000. In May 2026 the directors proposed a dividend of ₹1,00,000 for 2025-26. Its net profit before tax is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹3,20,000. 80,000 + 50,000 + 70,000 + 30,000 + 90,000 = 3,20,000. The dividend proposed for 2025-26 has not been appropriated yet (a contingent liability), so it is not added.

questions.stem_md: Kasara Ghat Pumps Ltd, an imagined company, earned a net profit before tax of ₹3,60,000 for 2025-26 after charging depreciation ₹70,000, goodwill written off ₹15,000 and interest on debentures ₹27,000, and after crediting a profit of ₹9,000 on sale of machinery and a dividend received of ₹6,000. Its operating profit before working capital changes is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹4,57,000. 3,60,000 + 70,000 + 15,000 + 27,000 − 9,000 − 6,000 = 4,57,000: add back the non-cash charges and the finance cost, take out the non-operating gains.

questions.stem_md: Trade receivables of Thal Ghat Valves Ltd, an imagined company at Vaitarna, rose from ₹2,10,000 to ₹2,55,000 during 2025-26. In the operating section by the indirect method the change is

options.text_md: added, because the company is owed more
shown under investing activities as credit given
deducted, because ₹45,000 of the year’s sales is still uncollected
ignored, because receivables are not cash

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** deducted, because ₹45,000 of the year’s sales is still uncollected. An increase in a current asset ties up cash: revenue counted in profit has not been received, so the increase is deducted. A decrease would be added.

questions.stem_md: Fotula Dry Fruits Ltd, an imagined company, has an operating profit before working capital changes of ₹2,40,000. During the year inventories fell by ₹20,000, trade receivables rose by ₹35,000, trade payables fell by ₹15,000 and outstanding expenses rose by ₹6,000. Cash generated from operations is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹2,16,000. 2,40,000 + 20,000 − 35,000 − 15,000 + 6,000 = 2,16,000: a fall in a current asset and a rise in a current liability add; the opposite changes deduct.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Depreciation on the looms of an imagined weaving company, Pensi La Handlooms Ltd, is added back to net profit before tax in its operating section.

**Reason (R):** Depreciation brings cash into the business, like any other source of funds.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: depreciation was deducted in arriving at profit but no cash went out for it, so it is added back. R is false: depreciation brings in no cash; the cash came from the revenue that the profit figure already contains.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An increase in the trade payables of an imagined bakery, Diva Ghat Breads Ltd, is added when its cash generated from operations is worked out.

**Reason (R):** Part of the purchases charged in arriving at profit was still unpaid at the year end, so less cash went out than the expense shows.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: the unpaid part of the purchases is an expense without a cash outflow this year, so the increase in payables is added.

questions.stem_md: In the operating section of Anmod Timber Ltd, an imagined saw mill, net profit before tax adjusted for depreciation, amortisation, finance costs and non-operating gains is called operating profit before ___ capital changes.
questions.solution_md: The subtotal is operating profit before working capital changes; inventories, receivables and payables are adjusted after it.

questions.stem_md: Shencottah Timber Ltd, an imagined company at Puliyara, shows a balance in the Statement of Profit and Loss of ₹1,10,000 on 31 March 2025 and ₹1,70,000 on 31 March 2026. During 2025-26 it transferred ₹40,000 to general reserve, paid an interim dividend of ₹35,000 and the dividend of ₹50,000 proposed for 2024-25, and provided ₹80,000 for tax. Find its net profit before tax (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Increase in surplus plus every appropriation made during the year plus the tax provision: 60,000 + 40,000 + 35,000 + 50,000 + 80,000 = 2,65,000, that is ₹2,65,000.

questions.stem_md:

During 2025-26: dividend proposed for 2024-25 paid ₹40,000; interim dividend paid ₹20,000; provision for tax made ₹55,000. The directors have proposed a dividend of ₹57,000 for 2025-26.
questions.solution_md: Rebuild profit from the retained part: add back each appropriation actually made in the year, then the tax charge.

₹11,000 deducted in operating activities; ₹64,000 shown as an investing inflow

questions.stem_md: Dive Ghat Steel Ltd, an imagined company at Saswad, issued equity shares for ₹6,00,000 and paid ₹12,000 as underwriting commission and other issue expenses, which it wrote off against securities premium. In its cash flow statement
